content:
Yesterday it was reported that Apple had considered making a special version of the Apple Pencil for the upcoming iPhone Ultra, before ultimately shelving the plans.

Bloomberg pointed to three reasons behind the decision, one of which was a desire not to conflict with the position Steve Jobs held when launching the original iPhone. However, this is almost certainly not the primary deciding factor…

A short Apple Pencil designed for the iPhone Ultra sounds appealing on paper. The device is essentially an iPhone that can turn into an iPad mini, so giving it some of the same functionality seems only natural.

When Samsung launched the Galaxy Note phablet in 2011, it came with an S-Pen stylus. The concept at the time was that the device could partially replace a paper notepad, and the line continued for a decade with a loyal following before being discontinued in 2021.

Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman listed three reasons Apple ultimately abandoned the idea:

  • Storing the Pencil on the side of the device rather than the top would feel awkward when holding it
  • It would conflict with Steve's view that a stylus is an inferior replacement for a finger
  • It would leave ugly marks on the screen

I don't think the first reason is the main consideration, as mounting the stylus on top of the device would also have been a viable option. Although this would require an extremely short design, I believe it could still work.

I'm similarly unconvinced by the second reason. What Steve objected to back then was not the concept of a smartphone being usable with a stylus, but rather the notion that the model at the time had to rely on a stylus to operate. Allowing the iPhone to be operated flexibly with a finger was the real breakthrough.

In any case, Steve also publicly opposed adding a touchscreen to the Mac on ergonomic grounds, yet we currently still expect the upcoming MacBook Pro models to include touch functionality, showing that Apple is not averse to overturning positions once held by its co-founder.

I believe the third reason is what truly killed the idea. The surface of a folding screen is inevitably thinner and more flexible than that of existing devices. Apple reportedly waited a long time before launching its first folding iPhone precisely due to concerns about the screen's appearance and durability; having an Apple Pencil repeatedly scratching the surface would affect both.

If Apple could ultimately resolve this issue, would you like to see an Apple Pencil Mini designed specifically for a future iPhone Ultra? Let us know in the comments.
